For example, although a husband, wife, and daughter are three people, when classified as male and female there are only two categories. Likewise, stagnant neutrality belongs to the nonvirtuous side.

Vajra statement. Lord Taktsa says that conceptual thoughts arise simultaneously, their number equaling the number of external objects. But two or more conceptual thoughts cannot engage simultaneously: otherwise virtue and nonvirtue should also arise together, yet they exclude one another, like the tactile sensations of heat and cold. The Questions of Śrīmālā says:

Virtuous ordinary mind too is momentary;
Nonvirtuous ordinary mind too is momentary.

Moreover, if external objects are accepted, the reasoning that refutes the Sautrāntika position of equal numbers of apprehended objects and apprehending subjects applies; if they are denied, the reasoning that refutes the true-aspect Ordinary Mind Only position applies. The Adornment of the Middle Way refutes these positions with passages beginning “If that is so, white and so forth …,” “The very nature of particles, white and so forth …,” “If according to the number of aspects …,” and “If that manifold were one ….” It would also follow that a single individual had many continua of knowing.[^N-A-069]

notes.problem: The text abbreviates two doctrinal positions and does not repeat the verb of refutation for the first.
notes.treatment: The shared refutation is supplied from the coordinated syntax. Ordinary Mind Only remains the provisional compound rendering used in section one.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. Elsewhere it is held that mental factors arise from ordinary mind as their basis.[^N-A-070] The Differentiation of the Middle and Extremes says, “There, seeing the object is consciousness; its distinctions ….” Accordingly, ordinary mind is explained with reference to the object about which superimposition has been cut off, while the subsequent conceptualizing and investigation of its distinctive features are explained as mental factors.[^N-A-071]

notes.problem: The active glossary does not establish the Abhidharma compound sems byung. The literal component mapping ordinary mind does not alone name this category.
notes.treatment: Use mental factors provisionally as a whole compound, while retaining ordinary mind for sems and basis for this non-ontological use of gzhi.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

notes.problem: The compact relation between the object, removal of superimposition, and ordinary mind is not fully explicit.
notes.treatment: Retain the object-relative construction without supplying a further epistemological account.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Here, accepting that mental factors arise from ordinary mind, we establish that ordinary mind also arises from them. For example, the thought “I shall become a follower of the Great Vehicle” is ordinary mind. Generating the ordinary mind [of awakening] on that basis is a mental factor. Through this, the Great Vehicle is established and the earlier ordinary mind is fulfilled: this is ordinary mind. In brief, the first instant directed toward an object is ordinary mind; the second, which investigates its distinctions, is a mental factor. When that is apprehended, ordinary mind arises again. Because these are taught to be a garland of instants, this position too is established.[^N-A-072]

notes.problem: The awakening orientation of generating ordinary mind is implicit in the Great Vehicle example; the next clause can mean fulfillment or establishment.
notes.treatment: Supply of awakening in brackets and render the earlier intention as fulfilled, without identifying the sequence with a particular later scholastic model.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. Others say that ordinary mind is what cycles in samsara, because suffering and karmic maturation depend on it, whereas the body is inert. Here it is held that the body itself cycles in the ocean of samsara. As its basis and support, it remains filled with seeds of beginningless habitual tendencies. When these meet conditions, various conceptual thoughts arise and produce a future body. It is like the great ocean, which serves as a dwelling and support for living creatures.

One may wonder how cycling occurs in the four formless states and so forth, where there is no actual body. Yet it is taught that in the formless there is non-informative form, in dreams a body of habitual tendencies, and in the intermediate state of existence a mental-faculty body. Therefore the body cycles.[^N-A-073]

notes.problem: These specialized classifications are not established as whole compounds in the glossary; the assertion about formless states should not be doctrinally harmonized.
notes.treatment: Retain the source assertion with provisional non-informative form, body of habitual tendencies, and mental-faculty body.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Supplement. Someone says that samsara has an end because there are no newly arising [beings]. Others say it has no end because it is taught to resemble a chain of buckets on a waterwheel. Here it is held that samsara has no beginning, end, or middle: its underlying character is not established, and the phenomena that appear are dependently arisen, free from all elaborations such as arising, ceasing, and abiding. As it says, “Whatever arises from conditions is unarisen,” and so forth.[^N-A-074]

notes.problem: The subject of newly arising is omitted.
notes.treatment: Supply beings in brackets as required by the argument about whether samsara can be exhausted.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. Dependent arising is the heart of all the Dharma taught by the Buddha. Awakening was attained through thoroughly comprehending its meaning. The City-Like Sūtra says: “Monks, when I sat at the seat of awakening, by placing this dependent arising foremost, I awakened to unsurpassed awakening.”[^N-A-075]

notes.problem: The fixed source reads byang chung where the formula would normally have byang chub.
notes.treatment: Render awakening provisionally from the repeated surrounding phrase, without correcting the Tibetan.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: In this account, externally a result arises when the cause, a seed, meets six conditions: the five elements and seasonal change. Internally, depending on ignorance as cause and the six elements as conditions, the forward sequence proceeds as far as aging and death; its reversal is the reverse sequence. In both cases results arise despite the absence of a self. Free from permanence and annihilation, dependent arising is like a structure of mutually supporting spears.[^N-A-076] They say that ignorance is just one of its twelve members.

notes.problem: The source names a spear structure, whereas the reference substitutes the familiar example of a bundle of reeds.
notes.treatment: Retain spears and provisionally supply their mutual support to express the stated dependency; do not substitute reeds.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Here all twelve links of dependent arising are the stirring or manifestation of ignorance alone. When ignorance is present, everything through aging and death is present; when ignorance ceases, everything through aging and death ceases. Thus these are ignorance’s stirring. The Condensed Perfection of Discerning Knowing refers to this in “Whatever beings are inferior, middling, or supreme ….” When ignorance is defeated by uncontaminated discerning knowing born of cultivation, all uncontaminated qualities are attained, as in “All the ways, doors, methods, and roots of primordial knowing ….” Grasping an object of focus as having defining signs empowers ignorance; the other eleven have no independence.

Vajra statement. Others explain that the twelve links of dependent arising fall into three groups: “The first, eighth, and ninth are afflictions; the second and tenth are karma; the remaining ones are suffering.”[^N-A-077]

notes.problem: The introduction reads literally along the lines of concerning others’ knowing and is syntactically irregular.
notes.treatment: Render an introduction to the opposing explanation provisionally.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: They say that these are completed successively across three [lives]: previous, present, and future. Here those twelve too—“They say that these are completed successively across three [lives]: previous, present, and future. Here those twelve too”—[^N-A-078] can also occur in their entirety within a single instant. When a conceptual thought of hatred arises under the power of ignorance, its initial preparatory phase is the affliction portion; the actual phase is conditioned activity, the karma portion; and its subsequent subsiding is the suffering portion. Thus all are established to occur between the arising and cessation of a single conceptual thought.[^N-A-079]

notes.problem: Two clauses are repeated verbatim, interrupting the transition to the author’s position; lhag is also awkward in this construction.
notes.treatment: Preserve the duplicated clauses visibly as a source repetition and supply lives in brackets. No deletion or Tibetan repair is made.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

notes.problem: The division between conditioned activity and the karma portion is compressed; the suffering phrase contains the spelling sdug ’sngal.
notes.treatment: Read the three portions in sequence, preserving the source’s explanation without silently converting ’du byas to ’du byed.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. Many differing accounts of the world’s dimensions, origin, formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness occur in the Kālacakra, the Arrangement of Hayagrīva [title uncertain], Vinaya, Designation, Close Applications of Mindfulness, and so forth.[^N-A-080] They say there are two kinds: accounts given poetically and accounts given according to the natural state.

notes.problem: The Hayagrīva title and segmentation of Vinaya/Designation are uncertain.
notes.treatment: Give a provisional partial title with an explicit uncertainty marker; treat Vinaya and Designation as separate citations pending bibliographic checking.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Here appearances differ because ordinary minds differ. Ultimately, neither environment nor inhabitants are established. For those whose vision is limited, however, appearances are produced by differing elements and phenomena of habitual tendencies, according to the particular ways merit has been accumulated. The Vajra Tent says:

The distinctions of objects and faculties
Have no separate aspects.
What appears as form and so forth
Appears solely as one’s own ordinary mind.

Furthermore, the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says that, of one commonly viewed [world], Śāriputra saw ravines, while Brahmā Ralpachen saw a completely pure field. Entering Bodhisattva Activity likewise asks, “Who made the ground of burning iron?” and so forth. It is like the different ways beings of the six migrations see water.[^N-A-081]

notes.problem: The shared object is implicit, and the following ragged terrain expression reads rang rong rather than an unambiguous familiar spelling.
notes.treatment: Supply world in brackets; render the terrain provisionally as ravines.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. They say that happiness and suffering depend solely on past karma, and that this karma does not change even when conditions are brought about. Here that is not certain: one may also enjoy the result of actions performed right now. Since all phenomena depend on conditions and are momentary, if one now acts to please a lama or king, one obtains a choice [or instructions?] and a reward;[^N-A-082] if one displeases them, the reverse occurs. This is established as a difference between pleasing and displeasing them, without depending solely on past karma. If everything were past karma, that would be the position of the proponents of [a prior] cause. Abandon it!

notes.problem: The source reads choice, where the lama/king parallel may suggest instructions, but that would require another reading.
notes.treatment: Preserve choice and show instructions only as a bracketed uncertain alternative. The source is not corrected.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. Others say that the increase and decline of aeons occur through the course of intrinsic nature: during increase, no means can cause decline, and during decline, no means can cause increase. Here the increase and decline of an age can be affected even now, for their causes are virtue and nonvirtue. When the lifespan declined from eighty thousand years to eighty, our teacher took birth as the caṇḍāla Great Strength and proclaimed, “Whoever takes a sentient being’s life, I shall take that person’s life.” Gradually establishing people in the sixteen principles, he is said to have caused the lifespan to increase to five hundred years. This is like a seed sprouting when water, manure, warmth, and moisture come together.

Vajra statement. Someone says: “At the present time, apart from what is experienced after rebirth and what will be experienced on another occasion, a result in this visible life occurs.” [The objection’s wording is uncertain.][^N-A-083]

notes.problem: The affirmative statement that a visible-life result occurs does not clearly contrast with the following response; a missing negative is possible but unverified.
notes.treatment: Retain the affirmative wording and display the uncertainty, rather than silently translating a negative.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: In the present discussion, results in this visible life arise predominantly in this very lifetime. Ajātaśatru asked, “What is a result in this visible life?” [The Buddha] replied, “If a lowly subject of yours went forth under me and came before you, would you treat that person as lowly?” He answered, “Far from it! I would bow and offer service.” “That,” [the Buddha] said, “is a result in this visible life.”

Likewise, even now it is established by direct perception that, for the most part, those who go forth, generate the ordinary mind of awakening, and enter mantra enjoy results in this visible life.[^N-A-084]

notes.problem: The whole awakening-mind compound has no approved glossary row.
notes.treatment: Retain the provisional ordinary mind of awakening from section one, preserving the established ordinary mind commitment for sems.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. In addition to the ten virtues, recognizing one’s father, mother, ascetics, and brahmins makes four; serving elders and giving generously make sixteen human principles. They say that spiritual Dharma is something different.[^N-A-085]

notes.problem: The paired terms mi chos and lha chos have no approved whole-expression mappings. Literal divine Dharma could misleadingly restrict the latter to gods.
notes.treatment: Use human principles and spiritual Dharma provisionally for the ethical/religious distinction being debated.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english:
“Expertise in human principles is spiritual Dharma;
Skill in conforming is hypocrisy.”[^N-A-086]

notes.problem: As transmitted, the quoted affirmative first line appears to contradict the preceding claim of difference.
notes.treatment: Keep the affirmation, without inserting a negative.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: They claim this was taught. Here, in all three sets of vows of spiritual Dharma, there is nothing else to affirm or deny beyond these, when one’s intention is to transcend samsara for the sake of others. Possessing these is alike in producing everything from the smallest qualities of human principles to the supreme accomplishment; lacking them is alike in producing a mass of faults and suffering. Master Ārya says:

“Having practiced human principles well,
[One reaches] the realm of the gods …,” and so forth.[^N-A-087]

notes.problem: The source quotes only the opening of the second verse line before returning to prose.
notes.treatment: Keep the quotation incomplete; supply one reaches in brackets solely to connect its named destination.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Thus the sixteen human principles and spiritual Dharma are established as equal in their essential point or meaning.

Vajra statement. Although the scriptures give many accounts of the teaching’s duration, the commentator on the Hundred Thousand says that, of ten periods of five hundred years, the first three are the times for attaining the results of arhatship, nonreturning, and once-returning together with stream-entry, respectively.[^N-A-088] The middle three are times of practice endowed with discerning knowing, deep absorption, and ethical discipline. The last three are the times of Abhidharma, sūtra, and Vinaya—the times of scripture. They say that results do not arise now because this is the sūtra period.

notes.problem: The passage names ten periods but enumerates three groups of three; its first group names four attainment levels.
notes.treatment: Preserve ten and all named levels, provisionally grouping once-returning and stream-entry in the third period. No tenth period is supplied.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Here, because the Three Jewels are permanent, whenever there are practitioners, attainment of results occurs without interruption. The Moon Essence Sūtra says that, as the teaching declines, the arhat Surata will appear during King Pungmarchen’s reign; and the Closing Period of the Wrathful Female [text?] says that, when the lifespan is ten years, two arhats will appear during King Dotachen’s reign.[^N-A-089] If one does not practice, however, one does not attain [the result] even while the Buddha is present, as with Devadatta and Sunakṣatra.

notes.problem: The phrase may name a text, but its identity and the exact division between the cited predictions are unverified.
notes.treatment: Treat it provisionally as a second citation, visibly marking the title as uncertain; retain the two reigns and the number two in the latter prediction.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: The Golden Light also says, “The Buddha does not pass into final nirvana.” Liberation arises without interruption until samsara is emptied. Classification into four periods indicates only greater or lesser prevalence, or principal and subsidiary emphasis; the succession of attainment of results is never cut off.

Vajra statement. They hold that, among the three trainings, training in ethical discipline must come first. Citing “Through special insight thoroughly endowed with calm abiding …,” they say the order is fixed.

Here [the source says] “it is fixed exclusively thus,” yet the five excellent companions received full ordination by comprehending primordial knowing, and Yaśas, son of the foremost householder, attained arhatship while still wearing a householder’s clothing and went forth later.[^N-A-090] Distinguishing these cases, the Basis says, “Like an adornment upon an adornment …,” while the Condensed Perfection of Discerning Knowing says, “Discerning knowing precedes the giving of gifts ….” Thus there are also cases in which training in discerning knowing comes first.

notes.problem: The affirmative claim of an exclusive fixed order conflicts with the counterexamples and conclusion; a lost negation is possible but unverified. The abbreviated citation gzhi is also unidentified.
notes.treatment: Expose the transmitted affirmation with a source attribution instead of silently negating it; retain Basis as a provisional title.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. As for the stages of the sūtra and mantra paths, mantra has the five stages, six applications, and so forth, while the vehicle of characteristics has three stages. Some Kadampas say that one first cultivates death, impermanence, karmic cause and result, the defects of samsara, and the generation stage for twelve years each, and afterward cultivates the completion stage for twelve [years].[^N-A-091]

notes.problem: The second twelve omits its unit; the preceding re distributes twelve years over the listed subjects.
notes.treatment: Supply years in brackets in the second occurrence. Generation stage, completion stage, and six applications are provisional whole-expression technical renderings.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Here all stages of the path must be practiced even within a single session. If one does not first cultivate impermanence in the opening period, one will wander aimlessly in the world. If one does not next cultivate karmic cause and result and the defects of samsara, one will not be secure against wrongdoing. If one does not then cultivate love, compassion, and the ordinary mind of awakening, the practice will not become meaningful. After that, the main practice is indispensable: the two kinds of selflessness according to the vehicle of characteristics, or the generation and completion stages according to mantra. Without dedicating the roots of virtue to awakening, they are wasted. Practicing in this way within a single session is the enlightened intent of Jowo Je.

Vajra statement. Since the Gathered Enlightened Intents and the Hundred Thousand of Bön accept that only one Buddha appears in a single field, some say that is so. Yet countless buddhas have appeared: the manifestations of the wheel of adornment of the buddhas’ embodiment, speech, and awakened mind are limitless and endless [the transmitted phrase also reads “exhaustion”].[^N-A-092] It is taught that, within the expanse of a single particle, the deeds of buddhas as numerous as particles are displayed. It is also taught that countless buddhas appeared when our teacher expounded the Precious Collection and White Lotus.

notes.problem: The text has exhaustion (zad pa), where a familiar formula might have inexhaustible; the syntax connecting this to the wheel of adornment is defective.
notes.treatment: Translate the intelligible assertion of limitless manifestations and preserve exhaustion visibly as an unresolved transmitted phrase. Use awakened mind provisionally for the honorific thugs.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: The meaning of the Gathered Enlightened Intents citation concerns the completion of [a buddha’s] deeds in that field. The Bön citation is not established as authoritative scripture. The nondual tantras teach that Devadatta, Māra, and their retinues are buddhas.[^N-A-093]

notes.problem: The glossary’s continuum mapping for rgyud does not name a class of scriptures.
notes.treatment: Use tantras provisionally for the textual compound; nondual specifies its class. Supply a buddha’s in the preceding sentence to identify the actor implicit in the discussion.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: This is the second section: an explanation of the fifteen vajra statements and one supplementary statement summarizing the essential points of dependent arising.

Others say that the Vinaya basket is called “individual liberation” because it means liberating oneself alone; many therefore assign it to the Lesser Vehicle. Here the sacred Dharma of Vinaya is common to the vehicles. Even temporary happiness in samsara arises in dependence on the vows of individual liberation: “Through ethical discipline one goes to happy migrations.” The peace of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas requires a human body, and that body too depends on ethical discipline. Ultimately, the buddhas’ qualities, such as the powers, are taught to be results of ethical discipline. The Condensed Perfection of Discerning Knowing says:

Through ethical discipline, those who desire peace become noble.
Even abiding in the sphere of the ten powers, they do not impair ethical discipline.

Thus, from the qualities of higher rebirth initially, through the awakening of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas in the middle, to great awakening ultimately, all arise from ethical discipline. A Letter to a Friend says:

Like the earth for the moving and unmoving,
Ethical discipline is taught to be the basis and support of all qualities.

Moreover, take killing as a common example. It is worldly nonvirtue, a defeat for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, and like a root [downfall] for bodhisattvas. Since mantra teaches that the inhabitants [of the world] are deities, there is no greater downfall than this. Thus [Vinaya’s relevance] is established as common to all.[^N-A-094]

notes.problem: Root is elliptical and byang sems could name either awakening mind or its practitioner; the parallel with practitioners favors the latter.
notes.treatment: Use bodhisattvas provisionally as the whole practitioner term and supply downfall, of the world, and Vinaya’s relevance in brackets.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: As for the meaning of the word prātimokṣa, Vimalamitra’s fifty-fascicle commentary says: “It is called individual liberation because, by separately practicing the trainings in denying and affirming without mixing them, one actualizes liberation—omniscience itself.”[^N-A-095]

notes.problem: The source says fifty fascicles; the rough reference mistakenly says the fifth volume.
notes.treatment: Retain fifty-fascicle. The commentary’s bibliographic identity remains unverified.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: If merely mentioning individual liberation made something Lesser Vehicle, the scriptural baskets of bodhisattvas and mantra would also have to be lesser, because the term occurs in each. Therefore the Scriptural Analysis says:

Just as a tree’s roots are foremost here,
The basis both for growth and for sustaining the whole,
So too, for every collection of qualities,
Vinaya is taught to be the cause and root.

Thus it is taught. Vajra statement. Although [Vinaya] is held to be Lesser Vehicle, the Great Vehicle in particular is clearly present within it. The first cause for attaining buddhahood, generating the ordinary mind [of awakening], is explained in the Scriptural Basis of Medicines: when [our teacher] took birth as Öden and heard the word “Buddha,” [he aspired]:[^N-A-096]

notes.problem: Öden is presented as a birth identity, not explicitly as a realm. The actor and awakening qualifier are implicit.
notes.treatment: Retain the Tibetan name provisionally; supply our teacher, he aspired, and of awakening in brackets, without adopting the reference’s Luminous realm.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english:
“Through whatever merit has arisen from giving,
May [I] attain buddhahood in the world
And free [beings] from every fever of desire.”[^N-A-097]

notes.problem: The first line has a repeated arising phrase and a strained final construction. The aspiration’s first-person subject and the beneficiaries are unexpressed.
notes.treatment: Give a provisional aspirational reading based on the surrounding account of generating awakening mind; bracket the supplied pronouns.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: That text explains this generation of ordinary mind. In the middle, it contains the stages of the path that complete the six perfections: the manner of undertaking difficult activity, such as giving away one’s head, feet, and hands in five hundred birth stories. Finally, it also teaches dedication, aspiration, and the accomplished result through passages such as “Vast generosity …” and through the twelve deeds. These are also explained in the treatises.

Supplement. Others say that the Dharma collections are distinct because each was taught as the antidote to a particular object of abandonment. Here all teachings are said to be included even in each one of the three sets of vows, such as individual liberation. Their enumeration according to objects of abandonment is accepted, but as for how they are included, the Gsang Bsam says: “All Dharmas taught by the Buddha should be included in the two accumulations of merit and primordial knowing.”[^N-A-098] This is because the two, means and discerning knowing, pervade all three sets of vows.

notes.problem: The reference is blank and the source gives an abbreviated title gsang bsam whose expansion is not secure.
notes.treatment: Translate directly from Tibetan and retain Gsang Bsam as a provisional citation label without expanding its title.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. Some Tibetan Vinaya holders say that Vinaya means ethical discipline prescribed in terms of denying and affirming, to be practiced by śrāvakas. Here Vinaya is precisely the domain of omniscient primordial knowing. Of the ten powers of that knowing, the nine beginning with knowing what is and is not possible concern phenomena in their extent; the last, knowing the exhaustion of contamination, concerns them as they are. This ethical discipline of denying and affirming includes all nine powers of knowing phenomena in their extent. More specifically, it falls within the power of knowing karma and its maturation.

The trainings are prescribed through the vision of that primordial knowing. Practicing them actualizes the ten powers; in this respect [Vinaya] is the sphere of buddhas alone. Accordingly, translators and paṇḍitas write, in connection with Vinaya, “Homage to the Omniscient One.” It is also taught that, when practiced in this way, it performs the teacher’s own work:

“When I have passed into nirvana,
This will be your teacher.”
With respect, the self-arisen one himself
Praised it earnestly before the assembly of monks.

Thus it is said. One may object: “If ethical discipline is this omniscience, the monk who preserves it must possess primordial knowing.” Although it is not manifest, it is present as intrinsic nature. It is like calling a person who has committed an act of immediate retribution a hell-being.

Vajra statement. They list four obstacles: (1) obstacles to arising, including an act of immediate retribution, birth in Uttarakuru, and an emanated [form]; (2) obstacles to remaining, such as lacking parental permission; (3) obstacles to attaining qualities, such as illness; and (4) obstacles to being seemly for others’ sake, namely what is unseemly.[^N-A-099] They say that, among these four, if any obstacle to arising occurs, the vows do not arise.

notes.problem: This list is highly compressed. The numbered categories qualify obstacles named only at its end; the first lists examples rather than a single causal narrative.
notes.treatment: Preserve all four numbers and unpack the syntactic grouping provisionally. Do not take Uttarakuru or emanation as consequences of immediate-retribution acts.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Here it is certain that vows can arise in someone who has an obstacle. These obstruct the arising of the results of virtuous practice, not the vows. The Basis of Going Forth relates:

A householder’s son regretted killing his mother and went forth. He learned the three scriptural baskets. Since someone who has committed an act of immediate retribution is one in whom [the result] does not arise, [the Buddha] said, “Expel him,” and he was expelled.[^N-A-100] He went to the seashore, gathered disciples, and taught Dharma; many became arhats. When he died and was reborn in hell, the fire immediately appeared to him as a heated bathing house. On that basis he was reborn as a god, heard Dharma from the Buddha, and attained the result. This was the benefit of going forth: although the karmic maturation is said to last a great aeon, he passed to the gods immediately after his birth [in hell].

notes.problem: The expulsion verbs have irregular spellings; the object of not arising is implicit. Later skal chen is transmitted where a great aeon is expected.
notes.treatment: Read the verbs provisionally as expulsion, bracket result and the speaker, and give great aeon as a flagged contextual reading; no source correction is made.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: One may object that this conflicts with the teaching that Ajātaśatru and others who committed acts of immediate retribution saw the truths. In their cases, the strength of earlier causes prevented the condition—the act of immediate retribution—from obstructing them. An example of such a cause is the teaching that Ajātaśatru had made offerings to seventy-two tens of millions of buddhas.

Although inhabitants of Uttarakuru do not take up [vows] through conditions, they possess them as intrinsic nature, for it is taught that they are reborn as gods, meet the Buddha, and attain the result. Emanated [forms], such as the young nāga, likewise fail to attain the result in this lifetime; this does not mean that vows have not arisen. Thus vows are established to arise even in the presence of obstacles.[^N-A-101]

notes.problem: The passage uses sprul pa for a nāga’s assumed form; the precise Vinaya classification is not explained here. Vows are implicit in the preceding Uttarakuru clause.
notes.treatment: Retain emanated forms provisionally and bracket forms and vows; do not recast the nāga as an enlightened emanation.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. Many others favor defining the essence of vows as turning away from harming others, together with its basis, and similar formulations.[^N-A-102] Here the Vaibhāṣika account is accepted: their essence is non-informative form. Within the eleven [members of] the form aggregate, non-informative form has three kinds—vows, non-vows, and intermediate form—and this is the form of vows.[^N-A-103]

notes.problem: The defining phrase is compressed and lacks an explicit ablative after harm and its basis.
notes.treatment: Render turning away from harm and its basis provisionally, rather than the reference’s reversed claim of harmful wrong association.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

notes.problem: The threefold classification is transmitted irregularly; sd om ma’i appears where a non-vow member is expected. Informative/non-informative form is not established in the glossary.
notes.treatment: Preserve the number three and provisionally interpret vows, non-vows, and intermediate form; supply members of in brackets.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: At the actual [ordination], oneself, the preceptor, instructors, and so forth involve both informative and non-informative form; from the second instant, there is non-informative form. This belongs to the phenomena element among the eighteen elements and to the phenomena sense-field among the twelve sense-fields. Its aspect cannot be shown, and it is non-resistant. In abandoning what must be abandoned, it remains like a dam or embankment holding back water.[^N-A-104] The Treasury says:

notes.problem: The actual rite is implicit, and shā rag is uncertain; the reference’s dried apricot does not fit the water-retaining comparison.
notes.treatment: Supply ordination in brackets and provisionally render shā rag as embankment from its local function, pending source review.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english:
Those three, non-informative [form],
The unconditioned and the conditioned,
Are called the phenomena sense-field and element.[^N-A-105]

notes.problem: The quotation’s list is not fully intelligible in the transmitted wording; the antecedent of those three is uncertain.
notes.treatment: Preserve the wording and enumeration without restoring a familiar canonical verse. Bracket only form.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Thus it is said. The essential point in accepting precisely this is that all phenomena are the very forms of momentary intentions: whatever virtuous or nonvirtuous intention there is, [its corresponding phenomenon] is established as that intention’s own form.[^N-A-106]

notes.problem: Here de kho na nyid can refer back emphatically to the account just given rather than introduce an abstract doctrine of suchness. The final subject is omitted.
notes.treatment: Read precisely this provisionally and bracket its corresponding phenomenon to make the shared subject explicit.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. [An action] is complete when it has four factors: basis, intention, enactment, and culmination. Two accounts are given, one prioritizing perception and the other the actual object. Here all phenomena have three [aspects]: ordinary mind as their root, the karma it produces, and that karma’s maturation. Since it is taught that when ordinary mind ceases, karma and maturation cease, if ordinary mind is virtuous, the initial karma and its maturation are also virtuous, like a medicinal seed. The reverse is like a poisonous seed. Therefore the Questions of Surata says:[^N-A-107]

notes.problem: The four factors belong to an action whose noun is implicit. Gzhi is used for an action basis rather than an ontological Ground.
notes.treatment: Supply action and aspects in brackets; use basis provisionally for the action’s object and retain perception for ’du shes.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english:
From pungent seeds
Pungent results will arise;
From sweet seeds
Sweet results will arise.

And the Blessed One says, “Tame your own mind,” and “Ordinary mind is, of phenomena …,” and so forth.[^N-A-108] The Analysis of Karma teaches four possibilities, such as action performed but not accumulated. It is taught that there is no fault when ordinary mind is wounded.[^N-A-109] Thus, in every downfall, motivation, intention, and perception are primary—as in the cases of the forest monk, Tshokchen, Mi Skabs Pa, and Zangmo [the names and their division are uncertain].[^N-A-110]

notes.problem: Thugs is an honorific address to the hearer, not proof that their mind is already awakened. The next citation stops mid-phrase.
notes.treatment: Use own mind locally for honorific thugs, preserving the imperative; keep the second quotation incomplete without restoring a known verse.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

notes.problem: Literally a wound in ordinary mind may refer to mental impairment, but the source does not specify the category.
notes.treatment: Preserve wounded as a provisional literal description rather than supply a diagnostic category.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

notes.problem: This compressed sequence of Vinaya case references lacks secure name boundaries.
notes.treatment: Retain each visible component in provisional transliteration or translation, and mark their division uncertain.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. They say that the vows of individual liberation principally involve the seven abandonments of body and speech, with the three of the mental faculty abandoned incidentally as their accompaniments; hence these are “the seven abandonments with their accompaniments.” Others say that the three of the mental faculty belong to bodhisattvas, so only the seven abandonments are required.[^N-A-111] Here the three of the mental faculty are the three poisons; the karma they generate is evil, which individual liberation must abandon. The Scriptural Analysis says:

notes.problem: The transmitted spong ’dun differs from the seven-abandonments wording in the preceding lines.
notes.treatment: Provisionally read the intended reference as the seven abandonments, explicitly recording the irregular source without correcting it.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: “I … desire … for the sake of freedom from desire, [have] taught the Dharma of the full liberation of ordinary mind and the full liberation of discerning knowing,” and so forth.[^N-A-112]

notes.problem: The source repeats desire with three tshegs between occurrences; the first fragment is syntactically unintegrated.
notes.treatment: Preserve the interrupted phrase visibly with ellipses and bracket the English auxiliary; do not silently omit the first desire.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english:
“Do not do any evil.
Virtue—[x: source abbreviation unresolved].
One’s own—[x: source abbreviation unresolved].
This is—[x: source abbreviation unresolved].”[^N-A-113]

notes.problem: Three lines are abbreviated with literal x markers; the familiar complete verse is not present in the fixed source.
notes.treatment: Translate only the surviving words and retain an explicit x marker for every abbreviation. The rough reference’s restorations are not promoted into source text.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: And:

“When restraint of the body is good,
Of speech—[x: source abbreviation unresolved].
Of the mental faculty—[x: source abbreviation unresolved].
In every respect—[x: source abbreviation unresolved].”[^N-A-114]

notes.problem: Three further verse lines end in literal x markers.
notes.treatment: Preserve each marker and translate only the attested words, without restoring the known parallel verse.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Thus it is taught. On your own position, it would follow that the three of the mental faculty were not evil. It would also follow that what is attained through renunciation did not belong to the mental faculty. You cannot accept this: direct perception refutes it.[^N-A-115]

notes.problem: The pronoun what is attained likely refers to a vow or its restraint, but its antecedent is not explicit.
notes.treatment: Retain the pronoun without naming an unattested referent; render the relation to the mental faculty provisionally.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Therefore even good bodily conduct is of no benefit [by itself]. Just as extinguishing the hearth fire stops smoke from the window, restraining the mental faculty restrains body and speech; if it is not restrained, they are not restrained. It is as with a wheel-turning monarch, [in a case] generated by a fault.[^N-A-116] Therefore the three forms [of wrongdoing] of the mental faculty must be abandoned as primary.

notes.problem: The monarch example is unidentified and its causal phrase has no clear subject; the preceding bodily-conduct claim is contextually qualified.
notes.treatment: Keep the opaque example visibly incomplete, and bracket by itself, in a case, and of wrongdoing rather than invent its narrative.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. The Treasury says:

“When training is relinquished, when one dies,
When the root is severed, when the allotted period ends,
Or when both sexual characteristics arise at once,
The vows of individual liberation are relinquished.”[^N-A-117]

notes.problem: The final verb is gtod (direct/bestow), but the surrounding discussion repeatedly treats these as causes of relinquishment. Mtshan ’das is also an abbreviated expression.
notes.treatment: Render relinquished provisionally from the explicit framing, flagging the variant; interpret mtshan ’das as expiration of the allotted period, subject to canonical checking.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: In addition to those five, the Vinaya scriptures teach change of sexual characteristics three times, discovering that one received full ordination before reaching twenty, disappearance of the sacred Dharma, and occurrence of a root downfall: nine causes of relinquishment in all.[^N-A-118]

notes.problem: The line merely says knowing full ordination, with under twenty immediately before it; treating them as separate causes would yield ten, not nine.
notes.treatment: Provisionally combine them as discovering underage full ordination, preserving the stated total nine.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Here, however, some among those nine causes do not cause relinquishment. The Scriptural Analysis teaches four possibilities: relinquished but unimpaired; impaired but not relinquished; and both relinquished and impaired. It is through the third that [the vows] are relinquished.[^N-A-119]

notes.problem: The text says four possibilities (with irregular spelling) but explicitly lists only three.
notes.treatment: Preserve both the stated four and the three stated cases; do not add the missing fourth.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Those of superior faculties do not relinquish [their vows] at death. By restraining afflictions arising in ordinary mind and not following objects, their ethical discipline has become excellent. The Flower Ornament says:

When virtue, nonvirtue, and their maturation become habitual,
They become interwoven with people.
Even without deliberately bringing such things about,
They act in another existence as in a dream.

Furthermore, the Basis of the Island of Throne Legs [title uncertain] relates that a forest monk died and was reborn as a god. Although offered sense pleasures, he did not accept them because he had not lost his perception.[^N-A-120] Those of middling and inferior faculties likewise do not relinquish [the vows] in relation to the results of a future life.

notes.problem: The source gives an unusual abbreviated title or section label whose exact identity is unverified.
notes.treatment: Translate its visible components provisionally and mark the title uncertain rather than assign a canonical identity.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: If [vows] were relinquished at death, what use would preserving them be? They would not help when needed. The one-day observance is not relinquished in its aspect as seeds and habitual tendencies.[^N-A-121] When the Dharma disappears, all three possibilities occur: relinquishment, nonrelinquishment, and uncertainty. An example of nonrelinquishment is someone who exerted himself in Kāśyapa’s teaching and became Ājñātakauṇḍinya.

notes.problem: The source again has gtod rather than the expected gtong of relinquishment.
notes.treatment: Translate not relinquished provisionally from the sustained argument, recording rather than silently repairing the source spelling.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. Some others hold that a single root downfall destroys all vows. Here the Treasury says:

“When it occurs, the Kashmiris
Hold it to be like a wealthy debtor.”

Thus the Vaibhāṣika position is that, even when one downfall occurs, the other three [restraints] are not relinquished; this position is accepted here too. If one impairment impaired them all, preserving one would have to preserve them all. The scriptural statement that a single occurrence makes one unfit to be an ascetic concerns precisely that [aspect]. Therefore impairment in relation to the four defeats is like owing a debt, while “impairment” is like still possessing wealth [the second occurrence is uncertain].[^N-A-122]

notes.problem: Both sides of the contrast read impairment; the wealth comparison suggests a missing negative in the second, but that is unverified.
notes.treatment: Preserve the second impairment explicitly as an uncertain transmitted phrase; bracket the implicit restraints and aspect without silently correcting the contrast.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. Others say that, since a single downfall causes a fall to bad migrations, preserving one or two [restraints] makes no difference. Here even the result of preserving one kind can bring nirvana. With the mental faculty utterly clear in confidence toward the Three Jewels, if one undertakes the discipline of preserving that one kind so that no condition can destroy it, without postponement and without abandoning it even for one’s life, one will ultimately pass beyond [samsara].[^N-A-123] The White Lotus of Compassion says:

notes.problem: The transmitted object is khyon, expanse, rather than an explicit samsara. The opening and following quotation specify nirvana.
notes.treatment: Provisionally supply samsara in brackets as the intended scope of passing beyond, retaining the anomalous source here.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: “Even those who have gone forth in my teaching and then move about in households holding a child’s hand will, in this Fortunate Aeon, pass into nirvana without a single one being left behind.” Thus it is said.

Vajra statement. Others explain that the four root [misdeeds] are misdeeds by intrinsic nature in terms of their essence, while digging earth, touching fire, and so forth are prescribed [misdeeds] in terms of perception. Prescribed [restraints] protect those of intrinsic nature as a thorn hedge protects a mango grove.[^N-A-124] They say the two differ because misdeeds by intrinsic nature are always prohibited, whereas prescribed ones are sometimes permitted.

notes.problem: The hedge expression is irregularly transmitted, and the source’s tree-grove analogy is compressed.
notes.treatment: Render thorn hedge provisionally from the protecting-grove relationship; bracket misdeeds and restraints where the nouns are implicit.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Here prescribed misdeeds and those of intrinsic nature share one essential point. The Buddha’s primordial knowing sees the unfailing occurrence of dependent arising as cause and result. Having awakened to the essence of all phenomena, he is no creator like Phywa or Īśvara. With great love, his awakened mind is impartial toward all beings; without abandoning diligence, he removes harm and brings them benefit and happiness. Thus, whichever one fails to guard against—misdeeds by intrinsic nature or prescribed misdeeds—the faults inherent in that case arise. Those of intrinsic nature encompass prescribed ones, and prescribed ones encompass those of intrinsic nature.[^N-A-125]

notes.problem: The name of this creator figure is not identified securely in the supplied materials.
notes.treatment: Retain Phywa in transliteration without equating it with an unverified deity.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: One may wonder why [rules] were not prescribed for animals and why their faults were not mentioned. Prescribed faults arise in animals and turn them away from nirvana. Although the rules were prescribed generally, they were not stated specifically [for animals]. It is like a father who teaches his sons what not to do, but leaves aside one who will not listen because nothing can be done.

Supplement. It is held that each of the four Vinaya schools differs in some respects. Here the root of all schools’ Vinaya is certainly the four scriptural divisions alone, for the Buddha’s primordial knowing establishes those four divisions. Otherwise śrāvakas and buddhas would have equal abandonment and realization, because [the śrāvakas] would have prescribed each of the four divisions.[^N-A-126] This cannot be accepted: even a bodhisattva on the tenth level cannot prescribe them, much less anyone else. Apart from slight differences in tenets, all incline and converge upon training in denying and affirming. Scripture says:

notes.problem: The verb bca’ zhus is irregular and the agent is implicit.
notes.treatment: Render the hypothetical attribution of prescribing to śrāvakas provisionally, bracket the supplied agent, and retain the source for review.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english:
Just as a tree’s roots are foremost here,
The basis both for growth and for sustaining the whole,
So too, for every collection of qualities,
Vinaya is taught to be the cause and root.

Thus it is said. Vajra statement. They say that, because prescribed misdeeds and those of intrinsic nature differ, evil deeds and downfalls also differ. Here evil deeds and downfalls are the same, without a difference. Prescribed misdeeds and those of intrinsic nature are one, and the rules are held to have been prescribed for beings generally. Moreover, evil deeds and downfalls alike lead to bad migrations. The Scriptural Analysis says:

“A downfall is called a downfall because it causes a fall into the hells, birth as an animal, or the world of the Lord of Death.” Thus the two are like the terms “food” and “repast.” One may wonder whether there is also no distinction between subtle and gross. Both prescribed and unprescribed [misdeeds] alike have greater and lesser faults.[^N-A-127]

notes.problem: The statement can mean equal degrees of fault or that both categories admit greater and lesser degrees.
notes.treatment: Read it provisionally as both admitting degrees, consistent with the question about subtle and gross; bracket misdeeds.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: One may object: “An act of immediate retribution is said to obstruct arising, so that [the result] does not arise; yet for one who has gone forth, restoration is possible.” This too is possible, as in Ajātaśatru’s attainment of acceptance.[^N-A-128]

notes.problem: The name has mi skyes rather than the usual ma skyes, but the named attainment and earlier discussion point to Ajātaśatru. The objection’s syntax and missing object of arising are uncertain.
notes.treatment: Retain Ajātaśatru as a provisional identification; bracket result and keep acceptance unspecified rather than introduce an unattested realization level.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Section [source label]. Since prescriptions depend on conditions, they say that something prohibited initially is faultless when later permitted in dependence on conditions.[^N-A-129]

notes.problem: The label differs from the usual Vajra statement or Supplement labels.
notes.treatment: Translate Section visibly and retain the unusual source label without reclassifying it.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Here what is prohibited has always been prohibited, and what is permitted has always been permitted. What is to be rejected and accepted is determined as evil and virtue: these are the actions from which suffering and happiness arise. This is seen by the primordial knowing that knows what is and is not possible. Even compassionate concern has no other means of abandoning faults and accomplishing qualities without relying on this ethical discipline of engaging and refraining. Permission and prohibition do not turn one intrinsic nature into both virtue and nonvirtue. Nonvirtue arising from afflicted ordinary mind, whose result opens the way to harm, has always been prohibited; its opposite has always been permitted.

Examples include medicine for the ill, Śāriputra’s teaching Dharma to Paldenmo, and taking hold of the body of a woman being carried away by water.[^N-A-130] What was prohibited earlier and permitted later are distinct nonvirtuous and virtuous [acts].

notes.problem: Ro normally denotes a corpse, but the water-rescue context may use it for the woman’s body; the source does not establish whether she is alive.
notes.treatment: Use body provisionally without claiming successful rescue or that she was dead; bracket acts in the conclusion.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Supplement. They say that, apart from a downfall through contravening a prescription, there is no fault in losing seminal fluid during a dream. Here, even when loss occurs in a dream, there is a fault, differing only in being subtle or gross; both subtle and gross are taught. The cause, a seed of affliction, remains in the all-basis; depending on the condition of a woman in a dream, loss occurs. Thus it resembles an actual defeat or offense requiring a remainder [procedure].[^N-A-131]

notes.problem: The reference is blank for the causal explanation; sa ’on is transmitted where seed is expected. Pham lhag abbreviates two Vinaya offense categories.
notes.treatment: Translate directly from Tibetan with seed as a flagged contextual reading. Use defeat and offense requiring a remainder procedure provisionally, preserving both categories rather than flattening them to defeat alone.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Why, then, is it said to be faultless? This is taught through skillful means to those temporarily unable to accomplish [such restraint]; it is not a declaration of absolute faultlessness. If it were faultless, then sleep during the day, at dusk, and toward dawn—which is prohibited—would likewise have to be faultless, because the cases are alike.

Vajra statement. It is held that rules were prescribed only for the children who follow [the Buddha], fully ordained monks and lay vow holders, and not for other beings. Here, because prescribed misdeeds and those of intrinsic nature are one, the rules were prescribed for beings generally. Initially generating the awakening intention, gathering the accumulations in the middle, and finally awakening and [teaching] the Dharma wheel and prescriptions were undertaken for limitless beings, not only for followers. Thus the Extensive Display relates [his words] to the wanderer Upajīva:[^N-A-132]

notes.problem: The reference is blank for the addressee; nyer ’tsho names the wanderer but the Sanskrit equivalence is not verified against the cited edition.
notes.treatment: Translate the addressee directly, provisionally using Upajīva; bracket his words and the teaching verb required by the compressed preceding sequence.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english:
“I shall go to Vārāṇasī.
Having gone to the city Kāśī,
For beings who are like the blind
I shall make an unequaled light.”[^N-A-133]

notes.problem: The source has an extra ma in the expression for unequaled; the first two lines also run across an electronic line boundary.
notes.treatment: Give the contextually defensible unequaled provisionally and preserve the two destination clauses without harmonizing their apparent repetition.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: And: “Make a beginning and bring forth [effort]”; and: “Do not do any evil,” and so forth.[^N-A-134]

notes.problem: The second verb is quoted without an explicit object.
notes.treatment: Supply effort in brackets provisionally, without restoring the rest of a known canonical verse.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Why, then, are fully ordained monks singled out? They are taught as the principal recipients. It is like a wheel-turning monarch first instructing the leaders of the realm before establishing all his subjects in the ten virtues. If it were as [the opposing view claims], the Tathāgata would be a creator like Īśvara and would be partial. Therefore the Dharma king prescribed the rules for beings generally.[^N-A-135]

notes.problem: If it is thus could superficially point to the immediately preceding analogy, but the ensuing reductio targets restriction to followers.
notes.treatment: Supply the opposing view claims in brackets to identify the logically required antecedent, flagged for review.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. On the basis of distinguishing prescribed misdeeds from those of intrinsic nature, some say that preserving [the rules] benefits those who have gone forth but does not benefit others; likewise the faults of transgression occur for the ordained but not for other beings. Here any being who transgresses incurs a fault, and all who preserve the rules receive their benefits. Prescribed misdeeds and those of intrinsic nature, and evil deeds and downfalls, are not distinct; the rules apply to beings generally; and dependent arising as cause and result is unfailing. The arising of faults and qualities is described in the Establishment of the World and the Basis of Distinctions [titles provisional]:[^N-A-136]

notes.problem: The two compact expressions may be abbreviated titles or section labels; their canonical identities are not securely established.
notes.treatment: Render them provisionally as titles and mark that status, without assigning external bibliographic references.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: When people at the beginning of the aeon stored rice and so forth, many faults arose later. Likewise, five hundred non-Buddhist sages retained excess possessions, such as hides, and this is said to have obstructed their attainment of superknowledge.

As for benefits, the four great animals in the forest of Kāśī kept the established ethical rules and placed others in them. Through that benefit, all who died were said to be reborn among the Thirty-Three gods. The absence of specific mention [of others] is like naming the principal recipients even though rules are prescribed generally. Otherwise the Sugata would become a mass of partiality.[^N-A-137]

notes.problem: Nye zho is an irregular expression here; the preceding argument concerns partiality toward ordained followers.
notes.treatment: Render partiality provisionally from that argument, retaining the exact source for checking.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. Some reportedly think that, since prescribed misdeeds and those of intrinsic nature are one, preserving [the restraints] suffices without a rite. Others hold that [vows] are obtained by making a personal pledge before a sacred representation.

Here rites are especially important for entering the teaching. A rite is the teaching’s actual basis: when it is present, the teaching endures. Offering service and gifts of respect completes the accumulation of merit. Seeing the sequence of ritual procedures and their practice makes one skilled in what to do and what not to do. Taking [vows] before the preceptor, instructors, and community brings conscientiousness and a sense of shame. Therefore taking them in dependence on the persons [who conduct] the formal act of motion and three proclamations is profound.[^N-A-138]

notes.problem: The formal-act term is transmitted as gsol gzhi rather than the expected gsol bzhi.
notes.treatment: Provisionally interpret the four-part communal act as a motion and three proclamations, record the source form, and bracket who conduct.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Accordingly, scripture relates that [the Buddha] was asked, “After the Blessed One has passed into final nirvana, whom should we take as our teacher?” He replied, “Take individual liberation as your teacher.” And: “After I have passed into final nirvana, rely on complete rites.” And:

“When I have passed into nirvana,
This will be your teacher.”

And so forth. Vajra statement. Although desire and especially hatred are said to be grave faults among the three poisons, here unknowing stupidity is weightier than the other faults. The Commentary on Valid Cognition says:

“When there is a self, one knows an other.
From the division into self and other come fear and hatred.
Through connection with those two,
Every fault arises.”[^N-A-139]

notes.problem: The source reads ’jig, not the attachment term commonly expected in this quotation, and the following linkage is irregular.
notes.treatment: Render fear provisionally as the contextual value of ’jig, retain hatred, and do not restore a familiar canonical wording.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: The Condensed Perfection of Discerning Knowing also says, “All beings who are inferior, middling, or supreme—all of them, ignorance …,” and so forth. The Questions of Upāli says: “Desire is a small fault but difficult to part from. Hatred is a great fault and difficult to part from. Stupidity is both a great fault and difficult to part from.”[^N-A-140]

notes.problem: The source explicitly says hatred is difficult to part from; a familiar parallel may instead say easy.
notes.treatment: Retain difficult exactly as transmitted, without doctrinal or canonical harmonization.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: When this [stupidity] is present, one does not realize the meaning of selflessness. Without that realization, one does not know what to reject and accept within dependent arising as cause and result, and therefore does not transcend the result of bad migrations.

Vajra statement. Although the hells are held to be lower and animals higher among the bad migrations, here, taking animals as the subject, it follows that they are lowest of all because their stupidity is great. The meaning is this: although suffering is temporarily greater in the hell and hungry-ghost states, their duration is short, and many are said to be reborn in higher realms. Knowing where they have been born, through what cause, and how, they generate virtuous intentions; many therefore pass away [from those states].

Animals, being bewildered, foolish, and stupid, have none of these [opportunities]. Before their earlier suffering has been purified, they consume many creatures each day, creating causes of later suffering. Their time to liberation is therefore extremely long. Accordingly, the Close Applications of Mindfulness says, “Birth in the hells is easy [to emerge from]; birth among animals is not so.”[^N-A-141]

notes.problem: The quoted adjective easy has no explicit complement. The surrounding argument concerns duration and difficulty of escape, not ease of obtaining a bad rebirth.
notes.treatment: Supply to emerge from in brackets as the contextual reading, while flagging that the words are not explicit in the quotation.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Vajra statement. It is held that wrongdoing is grave for someone who has taken up the trainings, while there is no fault for someone who never acquired them. Here never acquiring them is held to be a greater fault than impairing them. Ethical discipline in denying and affirming is the antidote to samsara. Because it is difficult to practice, one may impair it on an occasion and experience suffering. Yet one’s initial ordinary mind intent on preserving it was connected through renunciation to the Three Jewels. Therefore the virtuous result of ordinary mind intent on abandonment will arise. The Sūtra of Mañjuśrī’s Abiding relates:

Mañjuśrī asked Śāriputra, “What meditative absorption do you practice?” and so forth. Many monks became greatly disturbed and fell into hell in those very bodies. Śāriputra said, “Those monks have been ruined.” The Buddha replied, “Do not say that. After briefly touching hell, they will be reborn in Tuṣita.”[^N-A-142]

notes.problem: The wording rgya chen may reflect an irregular expression for a large number, but does not unambiguously give a numeral.
notes.treatment: Render many monks provisionally; do not supply an unattested hundred or other exact number.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: Moreover, even if one temporarily enters nonvirtue, regret will cause one to turn back. A Letter to a Friend says:

“Whoever formerly—[×: source abbreviation unresolved].
Afterward … the moon … clouds—[×: source abbreviation unresolved].”[^N-A-143]

notes.problem: Both lines are abbreviated with literal multiplication-sign markers, and the second retains separated fragments.
notes.treatment: Translate only surviving words and keep both × markers visibly unresolved. Do not restore the complete familiar quotation from the reference.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: And: “Nanda, Aṅgulimāla ….”[^N-A-144] Vasubandhu also says, “Evil deeds committed unknowingly are extremely grave,” and so forth.

notes.problem: The source gives only two names followed by an abbreviation mark; the reference supplies two additional names.
notes.treatment: Retain the two attested names and an ellipsis. No additional names are restored.
notes.review_action: Check the reading and interpretation against an authenticated source.

english: The Vinaya also relates that Sunakṣatra put on a black woolen garment, said, “I am Bakula,” and threatened the Buddha. Indra asked, “Will even someone like this certainly come to be tamed?” [The Buddha] replied, “At some point, there will be a time.” These accounts establish the matter well.
This is the third section: an explanation of the twenty vajra statements and three supplementary statements summarizing the essential points of individual liberation.
